Pain
pān
n. (bodily or mental suffering; rendering Hebrew chil, makob, Greek odune, ponos)
From Latin poena, penalty, punishment, through Old French peine. The etymology preaches: pain entered the world as a penalty, and Scripture never treats it as merely mechanical.

Biblical Definition

Pain in Scripture is chiefly the pain of travail, and that is a deliberate choice of imagery. Isaiah reaches for it again and again — the nations are “in pain as a woman that travaileth” (Isa 13:8), and Israel's own futility is confessed in the same figure: “we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” (Isa 26:18). The image is exact, because travail is pain with an end in view, pain that is producing something. That is the difference between biblical pain and mere torment. David prays over his honestly: “Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins” (Psa 25:18) — refusing to separate his suffering from his sin, and bringing both to the same throne. Job feels it in the body and mourns in the soul (Job 14:22). And the canon closes by abolishing it: “neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” (Rev 21:4). Pain has a terminus, and a Person appointed to end it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pain first as punishment or penalty — the primary sense — and then as uneasiness or distress of body or mind, noting that labour and travail are its proper biblical figures.

expand to see more

PAIN, n. Punishment suffered or denounced; penalty. We say, a law is made on pain of death.

2. Bodily suffering; uneasiness or distress of body of any kind.

3. Uneasiness of mind; disquietude; anxiety; solicitude for the future; grief; sorrow.

4. The throes of childbirth. She bowed herself and travailed, for her pains came upon her.

Key Scripture

Rev 21:4 — "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."

Psa 25:18 — "Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins."

Isa 26:18 — "We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen."

Job 14:22 — "But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn."

Modern Corruption

Pain treated as the one self-evident evil, so that its avoidance becomes the highest good and any doctrine that permits it is judged cruel — the argument beneath euthanasia and beneath the denial of hell alike.

expand to see more

Make pain the ultimate evil and a whole theology follows. If suffering is the worst thing, then a God who ordains it cannot be good, and the doctrines of providence, of the cross, and of eternal punishment all fall together. The same premise, applied at the bedside, argues that a life in pain may be ended, and applied in the pulpit, argues that hell must be emptied. Scripture's valuation is different and steadier: pain is a real evil, an intruder from the fall, penalty in its root sense — and it is not the worst thing. Sin is.

Isaiah's travail-image supplies the recovery. Pain in the hands of God is productive, not merely destructive; it is going somewhere. Yet Isaiah 26:18 is scrupulously honest that pain apart from God produces nothing at all — all that labour, and the nation brought forth wind. That is the difference between chastening and mere hurt. And the promise of Revelation 21:4 is not that the saints will learn to reinterpret their pain, but that God will wipe it away entirely, having Himself borne the penalty the word means.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chil (H2342), to writhe or travail; makob (H4341), pain, sorrow — the word of Isaiah 53, acquainted with grief; Greek ponos (G4192), toilsome pain, abolished in Rev 21:4.

expand to see more

Hebrew chil (H2342) — to twist, writhe, travail; the standing prophetic image for national anguish (Isa 13:8; Isa 26:17).

Hebrew makob (H4341) — pain, sorrow; the plural stands in Isa 53:3, the Man of sorrows acquainted with grief.

Greek ponos (G4192) — toil, anguish, pain; named among the former things passed away (Rev 21:4).

Usage

"“Neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” — pain has a terminus."

"“Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins” — David brings both to one throne."

"“We have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” — travail apart from God produces nothing."
